title: Eight Weeks for When You're Not Sure Anymore
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for the believer whose questions have grown heavy. Doubt named without shame, the doubters Scripture kept, the old creed, and practices that hold you while a question stays open.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the believer whose questions have grown heavy. You may still pray, or want to, and still sit in church wondering whether that makes you a fraud. It doesn't. Doubt is not the same thing as unbelief, and these weeks are for the person who would rather keep the question inside the faith than leave in order to keep it. They're written by a pastor who came to faith from atheism and won't pretend your questions are small. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. The first weeks name the doubt and sort out which kind it is, then take each kind in turn: a question about truth, a silence where God used to feel near, grief or anger asking whether God is good, a wound the church gave you. Along the way you'll meet the doubters Scripture kept, psalmists whose complaints went into Israel's songbook and people who brought their questions to Jesus and were not sent away. The last weeks go down to the faith the church has confessed for centuries, and to practices that can hold you while a question stays open.

These weeks won't answer every question, and they won't pretend to. Some questions stay open for years in faithful lives, and nothing here will shame you for asking them. This plan isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the real people who can walk with you. If the doubt travels with depression, grief, or a fear that won't lift, bring in that help alongside these weeks. Walk them imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up.
careNote: If the doubt travels with depression, grief, or a fear that won't let go, or the flatness has spread to sleep, work, and the people you love, see a doctor or a licensed counselor as well as a pastor; if a church harmed you, look for a counselor experienced with spiritual abuse. In a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.why: You used to be sure, or sure enough, and now you're not. Whether it came as one question nobody could answer or as a slow quiet where God used to be, it has felt safer to keep it vague than to say it. The Gospel of Mark tells of a father whose son had suffered since childhood and whom Jesus's disciples had failed to help. When Jesus told him that all things are possible to the one who believes, the father cried out the most honest sentence in the chapter: “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus didn't make him choose between the two halves of his heart. He healed the boy. A question kept vague can only be dreaded, never prayed or examined, so this week you say yours plainly.
weeks.practice: Each day, write your real question in one plain sentence, the way it actually comes to you rather than the way you think a good Christian should put it. Be specific: whether the resurrection happened, why God went quiet after a death, whether anything your old church taught can be trusted. Then pray the father's prayer from Mark 9:24 aloud and add your sentence to it. No answers yet, only the truth on paper.

read.label: The care page on doubt, the ground these eight weeks walk more slowly

tool.label: Mark 9 in the Study Bible, where a father asks Jesus to help his unbelief, with notes and questions

weeks.reflection: What is the question I've kept vague, and what have I feared would happen if I said it plainly?

weeks.focus: Which kind of doubt is loudest
weeks.why: Doubt comes in more than one kind, and the kinds need different help. One kind is about truth: did this really happen, is any of it real? Another is felt: God once seemed near, and now there is a silence. Grief or anger can ask whether God is good, after a death that should not have happened or in the face of cruelty that prospers. And some doubt began with people, a leader who lied or a church that closed ranks. Most of us carry a mix, and it matters which kind is loudest, because a stack of books won't heal a grief and a kind word won't settle whether Jesus rose from the dead. The next four weeks take each kind in turn.
weeks.practice: Each day, read back your sentence from week one and ask what it most needs: evidence weighed, company in a silence, room to grieve or to be angry, or the truth told about what people did. Write the answer beside it, and do the same for any new question that surfaces. Before the week ends, tell one person what you've found, someone who won't panic or preach: a pastor you trust, a steady friend, or a counselor.

read.label: How to Handle Doubt, which begins by telling one specific doubt apart from the whole of your faith

tool.label: When Faith Has Questions, a five-session study to work through alone or with the person you tell, with sessions on God's silence, Scripture, and the church's wounds

weeks.reflection: Which kind of doubt is loudest in me, and have I been giving it the kind of help it actually needs?

weeks.focus: When the question is whether it's true
weeks.why: Christianity rests its whole weight on an event, so if your doubt asks whether any of it really happened, that is a fair question to put to it. Paul said as much: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). That makes it a question you can investigate as well as feel. Thomas missed the first Easter evening and would not take his friends' word for the most unlikely claim in the world. Eight days later Jesus came back, spoke peace, and offered him the very evidence he had demanded, and it is the doubter who says to Jesus's face, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). The Gospel of John says it was written “so that you may believe” (John 20:31). No argument gives mathematical certainty, but you are allowed to weigh the evidence slowly.
weeks.practice: On the first day, read John 20 slowly. Each day after that, read one chapter of the Gospel of Mark as testimony to be weighed, and write down one thing Jesus says or does that surprises you. Before the week ends, write the strongest objection you hold in one honest sentence, at full strength. Then test it against this week's reading, and let the reading be tested by it too.

read.label: Did the Resurrection Actually Happen? The historical case, the skeptical alternatives taken seriously, and a plain admission that it is not proof

tool.label: Test the Case, an interactive walk through the case for the resurrection where you raise your own objection at every step

weeks.reflection: What would count as evidence for me, and have I given this question the patient attention I would give any other serious claim about the past?

weeks.why: Sometimes doubt has no argument in it at all. You used to sense God near, and now prayer seems to stop at the ceiling. The Psalms pray straight into that silence. Psalm 42, a song of the sons of Korah, comes from a worshiper far from the house of God, whose tears have been his food while people ask him, “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:3). He tells his own soul to hope before he can feel hope. Psalm 88 never turns toward the light, yet it is prayed to God from its first line to its last. The felt sense of God comes and goes, and its absence doesn't prove that he is gone. Grief, depression, and exhaustion can also drain the feeling from faith, so if the flatness has spread to sleep, food, work, and the people you love, see a doctor.
weeks.practice: Each morning, pray Psalm 42 aloud, slowly. On one evening, pray Psalm 88 and let it end where it ends. Then pray one honest sentence of your own, even if all you can say is that you don't know whether he's there and you're telling him anyway. If Psalm 88 sounds like your own nights, tell someone today, and in a crisis call or text 988.

read.label: What to Do When God Feels Absent, on the dark night of the soul and why the silence is not a punishment

tool.label: Psalm 42 in the Study Bible, the song of a worshiper asked where his God is, with notes and questions

weeks.reflection: What have I been telling myself the silence means, and did that meaning come from God or from my own fear?

weeks.focus: When the question is whether God is good
weeks.why: Grief and anger raise a different kind of doubt, a moral question more than a factual one. After a death that should not have happened, or years of watching cruelty prosper, you may be asking less whether God exists than whether he is good. That objection deserves to be felt at full strength, and Scripture lets a worship leader voice it. Psalm 73, which bears Asaph's name, admits, “my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped” (Psalm 73:2), because the arrogant thrived while his own faithfulness looked wasted. Nothing turned until he went into God's sanctuary; then he confessed what had been true all along: “You hold my right hand” (Psalm 73:23). Even John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come (Matthew 11:3), and Jesus answered with what he was doing and spoke of John with honor.
weeks.practice: Read Psalm 73 across the week, a few verses each day, aloud if you can, and on two of the days read Matthew 11:2-11. Each day, write your question about God's goodness in your own words, at full strength, without making it more polite than it is. Then say it to God, as Asaph did, and not only about him. If a particular loss sits underneath it, write that down too.

read.label: Psalm 73 in the Study Bible, a worship leader's account of nearly losing his faith and what turned him

tool.label: The care page on why God would let this happen, if a loss or a grief sits underneath your question

weeks.reflection: What happened that made me wonder whether God is good, and have I ever said that to him plainly?

weeks.focus: When the church is the reason
weeks.why: Then there is doubt with a face: a pastor who fell, a leader who covered for someone, a congregation that closed ranks when you spoke up. When the people who spoke for God are the ones who did the harm, it becomes very hard to hear God apart from them, and that is a reasonable response to what happened. In John 9, when the religious authorities threw out a man Jesus had healed, Jesus went looking for him (John 9:35). He kept his hardest words for leaders who block the way: “You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces” (Matthew 23:13). I'm a pastor, and those words are aimed at people with my job first. What they did is real evidence about them. Whether Jesus is who he said he was is a separate question, and it deserves its own hearing.
weeks.practice: Each day, write two lines and keep them apart. On the first, name what people in the church did, plainly and at its real size. On the second, write one thing you believe, want to believe, or want to ask about Jesus himself. Read John 9 on one of the days. If what happened was abuse, or anyone is still in danger, start with this week's reading, and know that a crime belongs with the police.

read.label: The church hurt me, the care page for harm done in God's name, with what to do first if anyone is in danger

tool.label: John 9 in the Study Bible, where a healed man is thrown out by the religious authorities and Jesus goes looking for him

weeks.reflection: Which of my doubts are about the people who hurt me, and which are about Jesus himself, and have I given the second its own hearing?

weeks.why: Much of what cracks under doubt turns out to be smaller than the faith: a slogan, a promise God never made, a subculture's rules, a Christianity fused to a party. Many of us were handed those instead of the faith, and those of us who preach did much of the handing. Underneath is something older. Paul passed on to the Corinthians what he had received “as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The Apostles' Creed grew over centuries from the questions asked of new believers at baptism. It is short, and much that Christians argue about lies outside it. It is also said together, so on the days you can't say a line, the church around you is still saying it.
weeks.practice: Each day, read the Apostles' Creed slowly, aloud if you can, and mark each line: one you can say today, one you can't say today, or one you want to be able to say. Don't argue with your marks; they will change. If you're with a congregation this week, say the lines you can and let the people around you carry the rest.

read.label: What the Creed Refuses to Argue About, on the small center the creeds hold and the room they leave around it

tool.label: The Apostles' Creed, the full text with plain notes on its history and its loaded phrases, to read aloud each day

weeks.reflection: Which lines of the creed can I still say honestly, and has what I've been doubting turned out to be the creed itself or something added to it?

weeks.focus: Staying near while the question stays open
weeks.why: The Gospel of Matthew ends on a mountain in Galilee, and it keeps a detail it could have left out: “When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted” (Matthew 28:17). Jesus didn't sort the sure from the unsure before he spoke. He sent them all, and what they carried down that mountain was his promise rather than their certainty: “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The letter of Jude, one of the sternest in the New Testament, still tells the church to “have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 1:22). Some questions stay open for years in faithful lives. They are carried less by arguments than by the practices that keep a person within reach of God and his people.
weeks.practice: Write on a card the two or three practices from these weeks that actually held you, such as the father's prayer, a psalm, a Gospel chapter a day, or the creed said aloud, and keep them daily. Go to worship this week if you can do it honestly, and let others sing what you can't. If church is where you were hurt, a different congregation for now or a quiet hour with the Psalms counts. Show the card to your one person.

read.label: How to Hold Onto Faith in the Dark, on borrowing the faith of others and keeping the practices when the feelings are gone

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to choose a few rhythms you can keep after week eight, with the question still open

weeks.reflection: Which question may stay open for a long time, and what will keep me near God and his people while it does?
